topics.next_session_task: Paused on 2026-09-30 by the author's decision (decisions register, Research practice): CM1 and the GCM disagree on how warm and humid the air over land is near the ground, and no affordable option settles which is right. Carry comfort as the range between them (42 comfortable hours per lunar day on the CM1 rings' land in CM1 corrected for height, 387 in the GCM; both put the most comfortable land poleward of 30 degrees); the corrected GCM design case A28_dim5_moon and its products stand. Reopen with an independent GCM (ROCKE-3D) or new evidence on what sets the warmth and humidity of the lowest few kilometres over land. On 2026-10-01 two GCM runs tested its cloud: convective cloud thinned toward CM1's (A28_dim5_moon_thin_convective, convective_day_s 2400 s) warmed the whole Moon by 1.7 K, and low cloud added toward CM1's foggy nights (A28_dim5_moon_low_cloud, surface_cloud_rcrit 0.6) cooled it by 5.0 K, each about alike from the ground to 18 km, so the GCM's cloud does not explain the gap. What remains is how each model treats the lowest few kilometres: surface fluxes, boundary-layer mixing and convection (the GCM resolves the lowest 5 km with two layers), and the forcing CM1 takes from the GCM. The cloud runs also show the GCM's climate resting on its Earth-fitted cloud: 289-297 K and 121-387 comfortable hours on the rings' land across those settings. The highland box ran on 2026-10-01 at the author's go-ahead (box_highland, 44.7 S 246.1 E, climate/crm README, 'A box over the highlands'; highland_analysis.py): dry and sunny, 192 strict comfortable hours per lunar day rising from about 130 below 2 km to about 240 at 3-6 km, upslope winds of 1.2-1.7 m/s by day and downslope ones at night, the air cooling 1.1 C per km by day and 0.35 at night. That run's terrain build set its forcing by the corner column's heights (2.9 km). The rerun holding and forcing each column at its own height (box_highland_own_height, 2026-10-02, climate/crm README, 'The box again, each column at its own height') keeps the air at 2 m within 0.4 C of the first run's at every height and makes the low ground more humid: the ring's day-night forcing now cools and moistens its lowest kilometre at night, so mornings there are muggy and some cloud gathers at sunrise. It has 183 strict comfortable hours per lunar day, rising from 82 below 1 km and 101 at 1-2 km to 262 at 5-6 km (the corrected flat ring: 3, 71 and 175); the afternoon upslope wind is weaker (0.8-0.9 m/s) and 0.09 mm of rain falls per lunar day. Moving the hold to 8 km above sea level changed little. Where the work stood: The faster CM1 build (the author's decision, 2026-09-29) was tested on 2026-09-30 (climate/crm README; climate/crm/build_check.py): neither rebuild matched moon_omp bit for bit, both stayed within the spread of two last-bit nudges of it, and -O3 -march=native, 11-15% faster, is now every OpenMP build's setting (OMP_DEFAULT; moon_omp_o2 keeps -O2; MPI builds keep -O2, untested); the runner records each segment's executable and threads. unresolved: The 2026-10-03 review (climate/waves/review.md, results/review_checks.json) holds the assessment. SWAN's and SWASH's lunar handling holds; the GCM-forced runs carry ExoPlaSim's open-sea roughness, which follows Charnock's law at lunar gravity (ratio 1.000000 over 203,389 samples; 6.04 at Earth gravity). The wave studies cover Smythii-Marginis (2.7% of the standing water) and, since 2026-10-03, the nearside sea (50%); the South Pole-Aitken sea (22%) has no wave run. Every coastal and run-up calculation holds the water level fixed, while the geography tide product gives typical monthly ranges of 3.7 m over the nearside sea, 2.1 m in the South Pole-Aitken sea, 0.55 m in Smythii-Marginis and 0.78 m at the eastern headland; the inverse barometer adds at most 0.18 m and wind setup about 1 cm. The coasts are regolith, whose sediment moves at about one sixth of Earth's stress for the same grain. The largest uncertainties sit upstream: the 1-degree basin grid (41% local change at 0.5 degrees in the pilot), the T21 forcing with its lowest level about 885 m above the sea, and a single lunar cycle.

The nearside sea (climate/waves/nearside.md, results/nearside.json), 1-degree nodes, 300 s timestep, second lunar cycle after a first of spin-up: mean Hs 1.39 m over area and time (Smythii-Marginis 0.88 m), Hs >= 1 m over 68% and >= 2 m over 17% of area and time, largest Hs 4.91 m in Mare Imbrium (19.3 s mean period). Mean periods 8-15 s; waves run toward the south-west north of 10 N and vary with a northward tendency in the south. Swell carries 34-64% of the energy at the reference points. Coastal power has a median of 87 W/m and reaches 731 W/m on western Oceanus Procellarum. A month at four shores (results/shore_month.json) pairs the hourly waves with the equilibrium tide of 7 February to 8 March 2038, matched to the GCM's Sun at mid-month: about 3 m of range on the northern shores and 7.6-7.7 m on the southern ones.

An isolated continuation of A28_dim5_moon year 29 supplies 481 global instantaneous snapshots over 60 Earth days at three-hour intervals. The original 30-day export overlaps exactly in all 6,416,962 values, and recording preserves final climate state and ordinary output. The wave model now follows two solar cycles, excluding the first 29.53059 days and analyzing the second. Inter-cycle and seasonal occurrence, other seas, coastal winds, gusts and an independent 10 m diagnostic remain further work. CM1 ring products retain only days 29.5–59.0.

The shore study adds native 118 m LOLA/GRAIL terrain, a regional propagation grid, and local wave grids from 948 to 118 m. Two basin replays retain all 3,103,551 wave values exactly while recovering directional spectra from the second cycle. The east-northeast phase gives 1.842 m Hs and 600 W/m shoreward power on the western face, versus 0.228 m and 0.021 W/m on the eastern face. In a later west-southwest phase at 237 m spacing, exposure reverses: eastern Hs 0.771 m and incoming power 52.9 W/m, western Hs 0.250 m and 8.35 W/m. All 13 coastal cases meet their stationary stopping criterion. Boundary position, regional grid, wet-spectrum interpolation and directional controls pass the stated exposure bounds. The 237-to-118-m comparison has height differences of 2.84% at the 95th percentile and 39.09% maximum; local shoreline convergence remains open. The three phases supply stationary spatial references for the subsequent evolving coastal history. The 474 m history retains this local geographic uncertainty.

The weather coupling preserves GCM dimensional surface stress through SWAN's Wu drag law at fixed air density 1.4039 kg/m3. The GCM stress-closure density over the selected sea and week ranges from 1.3885 to 1.4093 kg/m3. Spatial and temporal density effects within the wave source terms, two-way air–water coupling and lunar calibration of growth and breaking remain open.

At 4.001 m/s, frequency refinement passes the 5% bound. The 2-to-1-second timestep comparison over 20 minutes to 2 hours fails for mean period (12.2%); the later 1-to-2-hour window passes. Doubling coastal child directions from 36 to 72 at 3.8 km changes final Hs by at most 0.57% and mean period by 0.31%. The evolving coast adds two selected-window timestep comparisons; further coastal and upstream temporal refinements and parent directional coverage remain open.

The second-cycle Smythii–Marginis record reaches Hs 3.375 m with mean period 15.84 s at the peak; Hs>=1 m covers up to 84.7% of the coarse basin. Mean local Hs over area and time is 0.880 m. The offshore reference has Hs>=1 m for 309.6 hours, with a 98.1-hour continuous episode. In the selected six-day comparison, halving the timestep changes metre-scale heights by at most 0.376% and mean period by 0.870%; time above 1 m changes by at most 19 minutes per node. Across all paired Hs>=0.1 m, maximum differences are 16.29% and 29.37%, failing the 5% criterion. A shorter preceding history agrees with the continuous run within 0.440% in Hs and 0.913% in mean period over that window. Of 708 second-cycle spectra at three diagnostic nodes, 129 fail the band criterion, with resolved Hs 0.118–0.507 m. Widening the frequency band, complete-cycle timestep refinement and finer basin geography remain open.

The native shore terrain has 234 active wave nodes below 10 m depth in the eastward 118 m case, with 45 reaching the Qb>=0.01 breaking diagnostic. Its sheltered eastern station has 8.88% of resolved variance in the highest two frequency intervals, exceeding the 1% edge criterion. Wider coastal frequency coverage and tighter solver accuracy retain uncertainty in short-wave periods and small-wave outliers. SWASH now resolves individual waves, reflection, breaking and wetting/drying on 1D rock profiles and explicit beach slopes. The rock information retains 118 m geographic spacing; the eventual sediment geometry, two-dimensional diffraction and currents, changing water levels and lunar physical calibration remain open.

The evolving regional and coastal models retain hours 0–1419 and report the second solar cycle, 708.73416–1417.46832 h. Western Hs peaks at 1.797 m with 142.8 hours above 1 m; southern Hs peaks at 1.534 m with 96.3 hours above 1 m. The eastern peak is 0.968 m, with 77.7 hours above 0.5 m and its strongest phase about nine days later. Western mean incoming power is 12.5 times the eastern mean. The local offshore reference at 92.84570 E, 2.34570 N has 203.3 hours above 1 m; the earlier 309.6-hour reference lies farther into the basin. Main new 1 m crossings follow the local offshore crossing by 1.24 h west and 2.34 h south, combining propagation, local growth and direction. Station histories use 15-minute sampling and spectra hourly; further cycles are required for variability between months.

The shoreline model passes linear dispersion, gravity/clock similarity, still-water and wall-reflection controls. Under the selected changing-history peak, the refined western rock has a 2.070 m 98th time percentile and a 2.401 m maximum run-up in 30 minutes; the southern rock maximum is 1.684 m. Western beach maxima are 1.099 m at slope 1:20, 1.080 m at slope 1:50 and 0.900 m at slope 1:100. The changing-history 1:50 grid comparison changes the upper time percentile by 5.19%, exceeding the 5% bound; its finer breaking reach spans 152 m. The western rock grid comparison changes the upper time percentile by 1.1%, while a second phase realization reaches 2.659 m. The stationary 1:50 reference beach retains about a 6% upper-time-percentile difference at half spacing. Finite sampling, phase, friction, breaking coefficients, low-frequency boundary forcing, gentle-beach resolution and continuous changing shoreline histories retain separate uncertainties. A laboratory benchmark and lunar physical calibration remain further work.

The 900-to-450 s coastal timestep checks cover 720–912 and 840–1097 h after 24 h of adjustment. The earlier window passes all four station bounds; main 1 m onsets shift by 0.47, 2.60 and 5.20 minutes offshore, west and south. In the later window, the eastern net energy-transport vector difference reaches 13.83% at the 95th percentile, exceeding 10%; its paired Hs>=0.5 m subset gives 8.12%. Independent spectral transport agrees within 0.552%. Upper-frequency edge failures occur in 1048 of 2815 eligible coastal spectra, all with resolved Hs below 0.752 m; every sampled metre-scale spectrum passes this edge check. The transient nests use one iteration per step. Across 2835 second-cycle steps the coastal log remains below its 99% iteration-accuracy target, while the regional log meets it 68 times; coastal and regional total-height boundary warnings occur 2424 and 1936 times. Further iteration and evolving boundary-position controls remain open.

The irregular-spectrum flat-water SWASH control at 0.5 m spacing gives up to 5.22% lower Hs and 6.28% longer mean period across its three gauges, exceeding 5% bounds. Six layers retain similar errors. Halving spacing to 0.25 m gives 4.93% height and 5.73% period differences, retaining the period failure. The source audit establishes that above four uniform Keller-box layers SWASH changes from discrete Stokes incident velocities to a continuum cosh profile. Layer comparisons include that boundary change. Two eastern common-band sensitivity cases explicitly remove 4.52% incoming variance; the main profile cases retain the 1% guard. With identical eastern input spectra, four versus six layers changes the upper run-up time percentile by 6.75% and maximum by 10.66%, exceeding the stated bounds. Absolute shoreline heights carry boundary and numerical propagation uncertainty.
